about: Phase state machine read by `eos status` / `eos next`. Per mode: ordered phases, each with exit criteria. The current phase is the first one whose exit criteria are not all met. Checks are declarative (no code): exists, glob_min, checked, tables, table_status, state, any. A step may carry `options` (a decision: the human picks, each choice lists its exact steps), `tip` and `teach` (one plain sentence shown with teaching mode on). Edit .eos/lifecycle.json in a project to adapt it; `eos update` keeps your copy if you changed it.

ideate.title: Ideation
ideate.goal: Pick one problem worth solving and write it down.
ideate.why: Most failed products solve a problem nobody has. Ten minutes of writing beats ten days of building the wrong thing.

exit.label: an idea note
exit.do: Write a one-page idea note (problem, who has it, why now)
exit.prompt: Help me shape my idea into docs/ideas/<slug>.md using the ideation pack. Ask me questions one at a time. If I attach images, describe what you take from each one and note it in the idea.
exit.tip: Do this in a chat with a strong model (Cursor's best model, or Cline in Plan mode) and attach any inspiration you have: screenshots of apps you like, sketches, photos of a paper drawing.

discover.title: Discovery
discover.goal: Check the riskiest assumptions before committing to build.
discover.why: A brief with users, alternatives and a success metric keeps every later decision honest.

exit.label: a product brief
exit.prompt: Draft docs/discovery/brief.md with the discovery pack: users, problem, alternatives, success metric, riskiest assumptions.
exit.tip: Do this in a chat with a strong model (Cursor's best model, or Cline in Plan mode) and attach any inspiration you have: screenshots of apps you like, sketches, photos of a paper drawing.

define.title: Requirements
define.goal: Agree what version 1 does, and what it does not.
define.why: Written requirements with acceptance criteria are what tests and reviews are checked against; without them 'done' is an opinion.

exit.label: approved requirements (PRD)
exit.do: Write the requirements (PRD) and get them approved
exit.prompt: Turn the brief into docs/prd.md with the requirements pack: scope, non-goals, acceptance criteria per feature.

design.title: UX and design direction
design.goal: Main user flows and a deliberate visual direction.
design.why: Deciding flows before code avoids rebuilding screens; a written design direction stops the generic AI look.

exit.label: user flows
exit.prompt: Write docs/ux/flows.md (ux-design pack): the 3-5 key flows, states and errors.

architect.title: Architecture
architect.goal: The simplest structure that meets the requirements, with the key decisions recorded.
architect.why: Decisions written as ADRs can be revisited deliberately; unwritten ones get re-litigated by every agent session.

exit.label: an architecture overview
exit.prompt: Propose the simplest architecture for docs/prd.md in docs/architecture/overview.md (architecture pack). Start as a modular monolith unless there is a reason not to. Include a '## Repo shape' section: one app, one repo with several apps (e.g. apps/web, apps/admin, apps/api), or separate repos, with the trade-offs and your recommendation; I decide.

exit.label: quality-attribute and failure-mode tables
exit.do: Add the quality-attribute and failure-mode tables to the overview
exit.prompt: In docs/architecture/overview.md add a '## Quality attributes' table (attribute, testable scenario, measure, design answer) and a '## Failure modes' table (dependency, timeout, retry, breaker, what the user sees). Use .eos/packs/ref/architecture/quality-attributes.md and resilience.md.
exit.why: A design is only as good as the attributes it was checked against and the failures it plans for; tables make both reviewable.

exit.label: first ADR (beyond the template)
exit.do: Record the first key decision as an ADR
exit.why: A decision written down can be revisited on purpose instead of re-argued by every session.

exit.label: the repo shape chosen
exit.do: Choose the repo shape: one repo or several, and where each app goes
exit.why: Where the frontend, admin and backend live is hard to change later, so you decide it once, on purpose, now that the architecture is written.
exit.teach: For one person, one repo with several apps is usually simplest: one place to clone, one set of checks, and a change that touches frontend and backend is one commit. Separate repos pay off when different people or teams own and release the parts on their own. Your call; nothing forces either.
exit.prompt: Read docs/architecture/overview.md and the ADRs. Recommend a repo shape for this project (one app, one repo with several apps such as apps/web, apps/admin, apps/api, or separate repos) with the trade-offs for a team of my size. Don't create folders or repos; I decide.

options.label: One repo, several apps (monorepo) in this folder
steps: put each app in its own folder: apps/web, apps/admin, apps/api (shared code in packages/)
eos update   (again once the apps have code: it adds the checks for their languages)

options.label: One app in this repo
steps: eos update   (again once there is code)

options.label: Separate repos (one per app); this folder keeps the plans and becomes the workspace
steps: for each app, e.g. web, then api:  mkdir web  /  cd web  /  git init  /  eos init  /  cd ..
add each app folder (web/, api/) to this folder's .gitignore (each one is its own repo)

build.title: Build (stories)
build.goal: Deliver the requirements in small, tested stories.
build.why: Small stories with acceptance criteria keep each change reviewable and each 'done' verifiable.

exit.label: stories
exit.why: Small stories with acceptance criteria keep every change reviewable and every 'done' checkable.

exit.label: every story done
exit.prompt: Implement the next story with its acceptance criteria as tests; run the full check before saying done.

ship.title: Release
ship.goal: A first versioned release users can rely on.
ship.why: A tagged release with a changelog is something you can roll back to and talk about.

operate.title: Operate
operate.goal: Know when it is broken before users tell you.
operate.why: An SLO and a runbook turn 3 a.m. panic into a checklist.

exit.label: an SLO or a runbook
exit.do: Write the SLO and the first runbook
exit.prompt: Define 1-3 SLOs in docs/ops/slo.md and a runbook for the most likely alert (operations pack).

operate.then: The product is live: switch to maintenance mode with `eos mode set maintain`.

adopt.title: Adopt (map the existing code)
adopt.goal: eos knows the project: map, baseline and plan exist; nothing of yours was overwritten.
adopt.why: You can't improve what you haven't measured. The baseline is the line that may only move one way.

safety-net.title: Safety net
safety-net.goal: Old violations are baselined (ratchet) and the riskiest code has characterization tests.
safety-net.why: A ratchet lets you start strict today without fixing years of old issues first; characterization tests make change safe.

exit.label: a ratchet baseline
exit.why: Recording today's lint/type violations lets you be strict about new code now, without fixing years of old issues first.

exit.label: tests around the hot spots
exit.do: Pin current behaviour of the most-changed files
exit.prompt: Read docs/eos/project-map.md (hot spots). Write characterization tests that pin what the top hot spot does today (migration pack). No behaviour changes.
exit.why: You can't change code safely without knowing what it does today; these tests catch accidental changes.

stabilise.title: Stabilise (P0/P1 items)
stabilise.goal: The safety and gate items in the improvement plan are done.
stabilise.why: Fixing safety and feedback loops first makes every later change cheaper.

evolve.title: Evolve
evolve.goal: Ship features in small slices; tighten gates as counts drop.
evolve.why: The ratchet only moves one way: every PR leaves the code a little better than it found it.
evolve.then: When ratchet counts reach zero, switch gates to strict: `eos gates strict`.

decide.title: Decide the migration
decide.goal: Why, what moves, and the seam where old and new are switched, written down and approved.
decide.why: Big-bang rewrites are where projects go to die; a written seam and slice list makes the rewrite incremental and reversible.

exit.label: the seam filled in
exit.do: Fill the seam and the slice table in plan.md
exit.prompt: Help me fill docs/migration/<name>/plan.md (migration pack): the seam, and thin slices ordered by risk.
exit.why: The seam is where old and new are switched; without it the rewrite can't be done in small reversible slices.

exit.label: an ADR for the approach
exit.do: Record the approach as an ADR
exit.cmd: eos new adr "Migrate <x> with strangler fig"

rewrite-safety-net.title: Safety net before change
rewrite-safety-net.goal: Current behaviour is pinned by characterization / golden-master tests and baseline metrics.
rewrite-safety-net.why: Parity means 'behaves the same as today'; you can only prove that if today's behaviour is recorded first.

exit.label: characterization tests
exit.do: Write characterization tests for the first slice
exit.prompt: Write golden-master tests in tests/characterization/ for the behaviour of slice 1 in docs/migration/<name>/plan.md. Record real inputs and outputs; scrub ids and times.
exit.why: Parity means 'behaves like today'; you can only prove it if today's behaviour is recorded first.

exit.heading: Safety net
exit.label: safety-net checklist ticked
exit.do: Tick the safety-net checklist in plan.md (tests, known bugs, baseline metrics)

slice.title: Migrate slice by slice
slice.goal: Each slice runs behind a flag, in shadow then canary, with parity evidence.
slice.why: Thin, flagged slices mean any mistake is one flag flip from being undone.

exit.heading: Slices
exit.label: every slice live
exit.do: Move the next slice forward (planned → shadow → canary → live)
exit.prompt: Implement the next planned slice from docs/migration/<name>/plan.md behind its flag, dual-run it, and record parity in parity.md.

cutover.title: Cutover
cutover.goal: The old path is off, with a rehearsed rollback.
cutover.why: A rollback you haven't rehearsed is a hope, not a plan.

exit.heading: Preconditions
exit.label: cutover preconditions met
exit.do: Complete the cutover preconditions (parity green, backup restored, rollback rehearsed)

decommission.title: Decommission
decommission.goal: Old code, flags and data are removed after the rollback window.
decommission.why: Leftover flags and dead code are the next team's legacy.

exit.heading: Slices
exit.label: old paths removed
exit.do: Remove the old path and its flag for live slices

decommission.then: Migration complete: `eos mode set maintain` (or brownfield if more work is planned).

baseline-ops.title: Operational baseline
baseline-ops.goal: SLOs, runbooks and a debt register exist for the live product.
baseline-ops.why: In a mature product the main risk is breaking what users rely on; SLOs tell you how much risk you can afford.

exit.label: SLOs
exit.prompt: Define 1-3 user-facing SLOs in docs/ops/slo.md (performance-scale pack).

exit.label: a runbook
exit.do: Write a runbook for the most likely alert
exit.prompt: Write docs/runbooks/<alert>.md for our most likely incident (operations pack).

steady.title: Steady state
steady.goal: Small, reversible releases; debt paid down continuously.
steady.why: Mature products die from a thousand drive-by changes; small flagged releases keep them healthy.
